reading.title: How Fact-Checkers Weigh a Surprising Claim
reading.purpose: Learn practical habits for deciding whether a dramatic online claim deserves your trust.
paras: Each week, an incredible claim—so wild that it feels hard to trust—races across online feeds. Maybe a post says a small town found a glowing cave under its gym. A credulous reader, too eager to believe without checking proof, hits share in seconds. A trained fact-checker reacts with an incredulous look, pausing in clear doubt until the proof holds up.

Fact-checkers live by a clear creed, a guiding set of rules built on checking facts before sharing. First, they check the speaker's credentials, looking for proof of real training, field work, or true rank on the topic. They also check if a trusted board chose to accredit the lab or school named in the post, proving that the place meets real standards.

Next, checkers ask if outside proof gives credence to the claim, offering solid grounds to accept it as likely true. One shaky rumor can fast discredit a site, hurting the trust readers once placed in its work. By contrast, a careful writer who fixes errors openly and cites clear proof does creditable work that earns lasting respect.

Over time, those steady habits build credibility, the hard-won name for truth and care that makes people listen. You do not need a press badge to use the same steps. Checking who spoke, what proof exists, and whether other sound outlets confirm it keeps your mind sharp without falling for every flashy rumor.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "credulous" most nearly means
choices: carefully checking university records before sharing a post
too ready to believe a claim without demanding enough proof
unwilling to trust any news headline written about a town
officially approved by an independent board of scientists
qs.why: Paragraph 1 defines credulous directly as "too eager to believe without checking proof."

qs.q: Which sentence shows how fact-checkers evaluate the person making a claim?
choices: Fact-checkers live by a clear creed, a guiding set of rules built on checking facts before sharing.
First, they check the speaker's credentials, looking for proof of real training, field work, or true rank on the topic.
They also check if a trusted board chose to accredit the lab or school named in the post, proving that the place meets real standards.
Checking who spoke, what proof exists, and whether other sound outlets confirm it keeps your mind sharp without falling for every flashy rumor.
qs.why: This sentence explains what checkers look for in a speaker: training, field work, or true rank on the topic.

ev.text: First, they check the speaker's credentials, looking for proof of real training, field work, or true rank on the topic.

qs.q: Why does correcting errors openly help a reporter earn respect?
choices: Admitting mistakes shows honesty and protects the reporter's long-term credibility.
Readers prefer websites that publish wild rumors and change them every afternoon.
Open corrections allow a reporter to skip checking university records in the future.
Independent boards only accredit newsrooms that publish glowing cave discoveries.
qs.why: Paragraph 3 contrasts rumors that discredit a site with careful reporters who correct errors openly, building the credibility described in paragraph 4.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Social media posts about local discoveries are almost always true if many people share them.
Only trained journalists with press badges can tell whether an online headline is accurate.
Checking sources, credentials, and independent evidence helps anyone decide what deserves trust.
Universities should stop accrediting small labs so fact-checkers have fewer claims to read.
qs.why: The reading walks through how fact-checkers test claims and concludes that any reader can use the same habits.
